summaries.example: Imagine finding a notebook labeled with a famous scientist's name. Inside, most ideas came from another scientist, but later writers changed some parts and added their own thoughts. The notebook would be more than a translation: it would also be an interpretation. This is similar to what happened with the Theology of Aristotle.
summaries.summary: The Theology of Aristotle is an important Arabic philosophical text from the ninth century. Its name suggests that Aristotle wrote it, but most of its material comes from Plotinus, another ancient Greek philosopher. The text was made in the circle of al-Kindi, where translators and philosophers worked with Greek ideas. It does not simply translate Plotinus. It rearranges passages, explains some ideas in new ways, and includes additions that are not directly found in the Greek source. Because of these changes, the text is best understood as an Arabic interpretation of Plotinus. It describes the highest reality as a source of the world, discusses intellect and the soul, and presents some ideas in ways that connect Plotinus with Aristotle. The text became a major source of Neoplatonic thought for later Arabic philosophers and theologians.
key_ideas: The Theology of Aristotle was written in Arabic, but much of it came from the Greek philosopher Plotinus.
It was connected with Aristotle because of its title and introduction, even though scholars do not treat it as a genuine work by Aristotle.
The Arabic text freely retells its source and sometimes adds new passages.
Its ideas about God, the soul, and the order of reality influenced many later thinkers in the Arabic-speaking world.
summaries.why_it_matters: This story shows that books can change as they travel across languages, places, and generations. A translator may also be an interpreter who chooses what to explain, rearrange, or add. Studying the Theology of Aristotle helps us see how Greek philosophy became part of Arabic intellectual life and how later thinkers developed older ideas instead of simply copying them.

important_terms.definition: A way of explaining or expressing ideas from one language in another language.
An explanation of what a text means, sometimes including new ideas or changes.
A group of philosophers who taught that reality has levels flowing from a highest principle.
A name used for a highest principle that is the source of everything else.

summaries.example: Suppose a student translates a difficult poem, rearranges its sections, explains unclear images, and adds a short note connecting it with ideas from another writer. Calling the result only a translation would hide the student's role. Scholars face a similar problem with the Theology of Aristotle: it preserves Plotinian material, but its paraphrases, interpolations, and organization create a philosophical reworking.
summaries.summary: The Theology of Aristotle is the most extensive surviving Arabic presentation of material from Plotinus's Enneads. It was probably produced in the ninth-century intellectual circle associated with al-Kindi, and its preface presents it as a work connected with Aristotle. The entry explains why that attribution is problematic: the text depends primarily on Plotinus, whose works were translated into Arabic and then substantially reworked. The surviving Arabic Plotinus is fragmentary, moves through the Greek material in a different order, paraphrases rather than translates closely, and contains interpolations. These changes are philosophically significant. The text tends to bring Plotinus closer to Aristotle by describing the First Principle as a creator, intellect, pure actuality, and possibly pure being. It also interprets the soul through categories that resemble Aristotle's distinctions among rational, sensitive, and nutritive powers, while retaining a Plotinian hierarchy that includes the universal soul. One striking addition argues that intellect's ignorance of the First Cause can be nobler than knowledge, because complete knowledge would imply an impossible causal superiority. Scholars continue to debate the text's precise formation, including the roles of translators, al-Kindi's circle, and possibly Porphyry. Whatever its exact origin, the Arabic reworking became a foundational source for later Arabic Neoplatonic philosophy.
key_ideas: The Arabic Plotinus materials derive mainly from books IV, V, and VI of Plotinus's Enneads, and the surviving passages are incomplete and not arranged in the original order.
The Theology is associated with al-Kindi's circle, but scholars disagree about how much responsibility belonged to the translator Ibn Na'ima al-Himsi, al-Kindi, or other members of the circle.
Its changes to Plotinus include Aristotelianizing treatments of God, actuality, and the soul.
The text presents God as creator and first cause while also retaining the Neoplatonic idea of emanation, or the flowing of reality from a higher principle.
Its discussion of a superior kind of ignorance concerns the limits of intellect: intellect cannot fully know the First Cause without wrongly becoming superior to it.
The reworked text, rather than a pure Greek original, shaped later Arabic Neoplatonism and influenced works connected with Proclus and later philosophers.
summaries.why_it_matters: The Theology of Aristotle demonstrates that intellectual history is not just the movement of unchanged books from one culture to another. Translation, selection, rearrangement, and commentary can create a new philosophical artifact. Its history also shows how Greek, Arabic, Islamic, and later Jewish and Christian philosophical traditions interacted. Careful study of the text therefore requires separating Plotinus's original positions from the distinctive claims introduced by the Arabic version.

important_terms.definition: A philosophical tradition influenced by Plato that emphasizes a hierarchy from a highest principle through intellect and soul to the material world.
A shortened or expanded restatement of a source rather than a close, word-for-word translation.
Material inserted into a text that has no direct counterpart in the known Greek source.
The highest principle in Plotinian metaphysics, understood as the source of all things and unlike ordinary beings.
The intellectual level between the highest principle and soul in the hierarchy presented by the Arabic Plotinus.
A philosophical account of the soul and its different levels or powers.

summaries.example: Think about a video game guide translated for a new country. The translator might change the order of instructions, explain unfamiliar rules, and add advice for local players. The guide would still come from the original game, but it would also reflect the translator's choices. The Theology of Aristotle worked in a similar way: it carried Plotinus's ideas into Arabic while reshaping them.
summaries.summary: The Theology of Aristotle is a famous Arabic philosophical work that became important in the ninth century. Despite its title, it is mainly based on parts of Plotinus's Enneads. Plotinus was a Greek philosopher whose works were translated into Arabic in the circle of al-Kindi. The Arabic materials include the Theology, the Letter on Divine Science, and sayings attributed to a Greek sage. They draw mainly on the later parts of the Enneads, and the surviving texts are incomplete and arranged differently from the Greek works. The entry emphasizes that calling them translations can be misleading. They often paraphrase Plotinus and include interpolations—new passages without a direct Greek source. These changes introduce concerns that fit Arabic philosophical discussions and sometimes make Plotinus sound more Aristotelian. For example, the highest principle is described as a creator and first cause, and the text sometimes treats it as an intellect or as pure actuality. Its account of the soul also uses distinctions resembling Aristotle's theory while preserving the idea of a universal soul. Another unusual teaching says that intellect's ignorance of the First Cause may be nobler than knowledge, since fully knowing the First Cause would seem to make intellect causally superior to it. Scholars debate the text's authorship and development, but they agree that this Arabic reworking had major influence on later philosophy.
key_ideas: The text called the Theology of Aristotle mostly comes from Plotinus, not Aristotle.
Its Arabic form is an interpretation because it changes wording, order, and sometimes adds whole discussions.
The text often connects Plotinian ideas with Aristotle's views about God, actuality, and the soul.
It presents a hierarchy involving God or the One, intellect, soul, and the material world.
Scholars disagree about exactly who created the reworking and whether some parts may be linked to Porphyry.
Later Arabic philosophers used this reworked text as an important source of Neoplatonic ideas.
summaries.why_it_matters: The Theology of Aristotle matters because it shows how philosophical ideas are transformed when they cross languages and cultures. Later readers encountered Plotinus through this Arabic version, not through an untouched Greek text. Its mixture of Plotinian, Aristotelian, and later concerns helped shape philosophical discussions about God, creation, intellect, and the soul across many centuries.

important_terms.definition: A philosophical tradition based on Plato that describes reality as ordered in levels, beginning with a highest source.
Restating an author's ideas in a freer way instead of translating every word closely.
A passage added to a text that does not directly come from the original source.
The highest source of reality in Plotinus's philosophy; it is beyond ordinary things and is not simply one object among others.
The thinking level of reality that stands below the highest principle and above soul in the usual Neoplatonic order.
A study of the soul, including its kinds, abilities, and connection with the body.
